newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN meetings to see new members joining.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN meetings to see new members joining.

text.p: The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) will hold its increasingly high-profile annual meetings this week that will see Burma and Laos joining the group and Cambodia banging on the door to get in.
Burma, under military rule, and Communist Laos will be admitted at a special ceremony on Wednesday ahead of the annual meeting of foreign ministers on Thursday and Friday.

Cambodia was in line to have been inducted as well, fulfilling ASEAN's dream of having all 10 countries in Southeast Asia -- a region of great cultural diversity and ancient enmities -- in the grouping.
But Cambodian Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's bloody coup against First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh this month put that plan on hold.
Hun Sen on Saturday dismissed efforts by ASEAN to find a solution to Cambodia's political crisis.
Ranariddh condemned Hun Sen for rejecting mediation efforts, saying it would bring about isolation, an end to democracy and a return to civil war.

Cambodia's Foreign Minister Ung Huot will press for a last-minute change of heart at this week's ASEAN meetings, which Cambodia will attend as an observer. Diplomats say Cambodia could be admitted as early as August 8, when ASEAN celebrates its 30th anniversary, or later in December when the group holds its annual "informal summit".
Cambodia's crisis has taken the diplomatic spotlight off Burma for the time being.
Western governments led by the United States lobbied against Burma's admission to ASEAN, saying it should be isolated because of its brutal crackdown on the country's pro-democracy movement.
But in the case of both Burma and Cambodia, ASEAN -- which now groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam --is concerned about China.
Beijing is Burma's biggest arms supplier and recently signed an economic pact with Rangoon.

Cambodian King Norodom Sihanouk has spent at least as much time in Beijing, where he has a palace, as he has in his own country in recent years, underscoring the close ties between those two countries. China fought a border skirmish with Vietnam to "teach it a lesson" after Hanoi invaded Cambodia in 1978.
ASEAN's enlargement is also driven by economic logic.
The grouping is creating a free trade area for its members over the next decade.
With a combined population of 450 million, Southeast Asia is larger than Europe and its combined gross domestic product (GDP) of $600 billion ranks behind only China and Japan in Asia.

The region is critically dependent on trade, most of it with Japan and the West. ASEAN's combined annual exports of $250 billion represents 40 percent of its GDP and its annual imports of $300 billion make up 50 percent of GDP.

The two-day foreign ministers' meeting will be followed by the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF), which will bring together foreign ministers from 11 other nations including the United States, the European Union, China, Japan, Russia, India and Australia.
The ARF has emerged as the premier vehicle for talks on political and security issues in the Asia-Pacific region.
Issues ranging from the conflicting territorial claims in the South China Sea, tensions on the Korea peninsula, Burma and Cambodia will likely feature in the discussions.

For the first time, defence officials have been invited to attend the security talks. Previous ARF meetings have been confined to foreign ministers and their senior officials because some countries had been wary of turning ARF into an Asian version of the European conference on security, diplomats said.

The ARF was set up four years ago as a way to solve potential conflicts in the Asia-Pacific region. It was supposed to evolve through three stages, from discussion of issues to preventive diplomacy and finally to conflict resolution.
Diplomats say it is stuck somewhere between the first two stages. "Right now it's more ARF than bite," one quipped.
Much of the real talking and dealing will take place outside the conference room in keeping with ASEAN's emphasis on informal talks aimed at building relationships and personal bonds.
